{{Short description|Result on gamma function}}
{{For|the result about ordered groups|Archimedean group#Examples of Archimedean groups}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Hölder's theorem''' states that the [[gamma function]] does not satisfy any [[algebraic differential equation]] whose coefficients are [[rational function]]s. This result was first proved by [[Otto Hölder]] in 1887; several alternative proofs have subsequently been found.<ref>Bank, Steven B. & Kaufman, Robert. “[https://doi.org/10.1007%2FBF01421399 A Note on Hölder’s Theorem Concerning the Gamma Function]”, ''[[Mathematische Annalen]]'', vol 232, 1978.</ref>

The theorem also generalizes to the [[q-gamma function|<math> q </math>-gamma function]].

==Statement of the theorem==

For every <math>n \in \N_0,</math> there is no non-zero polynomial <math> P \in \Complex [X;Y_0,Y_1,\ldots,Y_n] </math> such that
<math display="block">\forall z \in \Complex \setminus \Z _{\leq 0}: \qquad P \left( z;\Gamma(z),\Gamma'(z),\ldots,{\Gamma^{(n)}}(z) \right) = 0,</math>
where <math> \Gamma </math> is the [[gamma function]].

For example, define <math> P \in \Complex [X;Y_0,Y_1,Y_2] </math> by 
<math display="block"> P ~ \stackrel{\text{df}}{=} ~ X^2 Y_2 + X Y_1 + (X^2 - \nu^2) Y_0.</math>

Then the equation
<math display="block">P \left (z;f(z),f'(z),f''(z) \right ) = z^2 f''(z) + z f'(z) + \left (z^2 - \nu^2 \right ) f(z) \equiv 0</math>
is called an ''algebraic differential equation'', which, in this case, has the solutions <math>f = J_{\nu}</math> and <math>f = Y_{\nu}</math> — the Bessel functions of the first and second kind respectively. Hence, we say that <math>J_{\nu}</math> and <math> Y_{\nu}</math> are ''differentially algebraic'' (also ''algebraically transcendental''). Most of the familiar [[special functions]] of [[mathematical physics]] are differentially algebraic. All algebraic combinations of differentially [[Algebraic function|algebraic functions]] are differentially algebraic. Furthermore, all compositions of differentially algebraic functions are differentially algebraic. Hölder's Theorem simply states that the gamma function, <math> \Gamma </math>, is not differentially algebraic and is therefore ''[[transcendentally transcendental function|transcendentally transcendental]].''<ref name = "Rubel" />

==Proof==

Let <math> n \in \N_0,</math> and assume that a non-zero polynomial <math> P \in \Complex [X;Y_0,Y_1,\ldots,Y_n] </math> exists such that
<math display="block">\forall z \in \Complex \setminus \Z _{\leq 0}: \qquad P \left( z;\Gamma(z),\Gamma'(z),\ldots,{\Gamma^{(n)}}(z) \right) = 0.
</math>

As a non-zero polynomial in <math> \Complex [X] </math> can never give rise to the zero function on any non-empty open domain of <math> \Complex </math> (by the [[fundamental theorem of algebra]]), we may suppose, [[without loss of generality]], that <math> P </math> contains a monomial term having a non-zero power of one of the indeterminates <math> Y_0,Y_1,\ldots,Y_n </math>.

Assume also that <math> P </math> has the lowest possible overall degree with respect to the lexicographic ordering <math>Y_0 < Y_1 < \cdots < Y_n < X.</math> For example,
<math display="block">\deg \left(-3 X^{10} Y_0^2 Y_1^4 + i X^2Y_2 \right) < \deg \left( 2 X Y_0^3 - Y_1^4 \right)</math>
because the highest power of <math> Y_{0} </math> in any monomial term of the first polynomial is smaller than that of the second polynomial.

Next, observe that for all <math>z \in \Complex \smallsetminus \Z _{\leq 0}</math> we have:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
&P \left(z + 1; \Gamma(z + 1), \Gamma'(z + 1), \Gamma''(z + 1),\ldots, \Gamma^{(n)}(z + 1) \right) \\[1ex]
&= P \left(z + 1;z \Gamma(z), [z \Gamma(z)]',[z \Gamma(z)]'',\ldots,[z \Gamma(z)]^{(n)} \right) \\[1ex]
&= P \left(z + 1;z \Gamma(z), z \Gamma'(z) + \Gamma(z),z \Gamma''(z) + 2\Gamma'(z),\ldots, z {\Gamma^{(n)}}(z) + n {\Gamma^{(n - 1)}}(z) \right).
\end{align}</math>

If we define a second polynomial <math> Q \in \Complex [X;Y_0,Y_1,\ldots,Y_n] </math> by the transformation
<math display="block">Q ~ \stackrel{\text{df}}{=} ~ P(X + 1;X Y_0,X Y_1 + Y_0,X Y_2 + 2 Y_1,\ldots,X Y_n + n Y_{n - 1}),</math>
then we obtain the following algebraic differential equation for <math> \Gamma </math>:
<math display="block">\forall z \in \Complex \setminus \Z _{\leq 0}: \qquad Q \left( z;\Gamma(z),\Gamma'(z),\ldots,{\Gamma^{(n)}}(z) \right) \equiv 0.
</math>

Furthermore, let <math> X^h Y_0^{h_0} Y_1^{h_1} \cdots Y_n^{h_n} </math> be the highest-degree monomial term in <math> P </math>, and define <math> S = h_0 + h_1 + \cdots + h_n </math>. Because the transformation for <math> Q </math> substitutes <math> X+1 </math> for <math> X </math>, the leading monomial's <math> X^h </math> term expands via the binomial theorem to <math> (X+1)^h </math>. To properly cancel the leading terms under the lexicographic ordering, we must multiply <math> P </math> by a polynomial <math> R(X) </math> that accounts for this expansion. Defining <math> R \in \Complex[X] </math> as the polynomial quotient of <math> (X+1)^h X^S </math> divided by <math> X^h </math> (which, when <math> S \geq h </math>, is simply <math> (X+1)^h X^{S-h} </math>), the polynomial
<math display="block">Q - R(X) P</math>
has a strictly smaller overall degree than <math> P </math>. As it clearly gives rise to an algebraic differential equation for <math> \Gamma </math>, it must be the zero polynomial by the minimality assumption on <math>P</math>. Hence, we get
<math display="block">Q= P(X + 1;X Y_0,X Y_1 + Y_0,X Y_2 + 2Y_1,\ldots,X Y_n + n Y_{n-1})= R(X) \cdot P(X;Y_0,Y_1,\ldots,Y_n).
</math>

Now, let <math> X = 0 </math> in <math> Q </math>. Assuming the generic case where <math> S > h </math>, we have <math> R(0) = 0 </math>, yielding
<math display="block">Q(0;Y_0,Y_1,\ldots,Y_n) = P(1;0,Y_0,2 Y_1,\ldots,n Y_{n-1}) = R(0) \cdot P(0;Y_0,Y_1,\ldots,Y_n) = 0_{\Complex [Y_0,Y_1,\ldots,Y_n]}.</math>
(In the edge cases where <math>S \leq h</math>, a similar deduction holds by observing that replacing <math>P</math> with <math>P - P|_{X=0}</math> would yield a polynomial of strictly smaller degree that still satisfies the differential equation, thereby forcing <math>P(1;0,Y_1,\ldots,Y_n) = 0</math> directly to avoid contradicting minimality).

A change of variables then yields 
<math display="block"> P(1;0,Y_1,Y_2,\ldots,Y_n) = 0_{\Complex [Y_0,Y_1,\ldots,Y_n]},</math> 
and an application of [[mathematical induction]] (along with a change of variables at each induction step) to the earlier expression
<math display="block">P(X + 1;X Y_0,X Y_1 + Y_0,X Y_2 + 2Y_1,\ldots,X Y_n + nY_{n-1})= R(X) \cdot P(X;Y_0,Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)
</math>
reveals that
<math display="block">\forall m \in \N: \qquad P(m;0,Y_1,Y_2,\ldots,Y_n) = 0_{\Complex [Y_0,Y_1,\ldots,Y_n]}.</math>

This is possible only if <math> P </math> is divisible by <math> Y_{0} </math>, which contradicts the minimality assumption on <math> P </math>. Therefore, no such <math> P </math> exists, and so <math> \Gamma </math> is not differentially algebraic.<ref name = "Rubel">Rubel, Lee A. “A Survey of Transcendentally Transcendental Functions”, ''The American Mathematical Monthly'' '''96''': pp. 777–788 (November 1989). {{JSTOR|2324840}}</ref><ref>Boros, George & [[Victor Hugo Moll|Moll, Victor]]. ''Irresistible Integrals'', Cambridge University Press, 2004, Cambridge Books Online, 30 December 2011. {{doi|10.1017/CBO9780511617041.003}}</ref> [[Q.E.D.]]
